seo.title: Bathroom Survey in Windsor | £125 Fixed-Price Survey | Install My Bathroom
seo.description: Book a £125 bathroom survey in Windsor. We measure, check access and waste runs, and scope period town houses and inter-war family homes before any installation quote.

hero.intro: Before we quote for a bathroom installation anywhere in Windsor, we carry out a fixed-price £125 survey at the property. It's the stage where a floor plan on paper meets the reality of your walls, your waste runs and your access routes, and it's what stops a quote turning into a list of surprises once the fitting team is on site. Windsor's housing stock splits fairly cleanly into two character types, and the survey has to account for which one applies to your house before anything gets priced. Close to the Castle and the historic centre, there's a concentration of Georgian and Victorian town houses, many on narrow plots with limited rear access and period staircases that constrain how much material can be moved through the building at once. Further out, towards the edges of town, the housing is more typically inter-war and post-war family homes, with a scattering of newer residential developments on sites that have been redeveloped over the years. Those are two genuinely different sets of access and structural conditions, and the survey is where we work out which one actually applies to your property, rather than assuming it from the postcode alone.

sections.heading: What the £125 survey covers
sections.body: The survey fee is fixed at £125 regardless of the size or complexity of the room, and it's deducted from your project cost if you go ahead with an installation. On the day, we measure the room accurately, identify where the waste pipe currently runs and whether it can be moved or needs to stay put, check the water supply and pressure feeding the room, and look at the floor and wall build-up to establish what's underneath the surfaces you can see. We also check access — door widths, staircases, and how materials will move in and waste will move out — because that affects both the practicality of the work and, in some cases, the fittings you can realistically choose. In Windsor specifically, access is often the detail that most changes a quote, so we spend real time on it at survey rather than estimating it from photos. By the end of the survey you get a written scope and a firm quote, not a ballpark figure that moves once work starts. We don't ask for a deposit to book the survey conversation itself; it's a paid, fixed-fee visit precisely so that the advice you get is based on your actual property, not a generic estimate.

sections.heading: What that looks like in a typical Windsor property
sections.body: Windsor's housing splits fairly cleanly into two character types, and we survey each one differently. Close to the Castle and the historic centre, there's a concentration of Georgian and Victorian town houses, many on narrow plots with limited rear access and period staircases that constrain how much material can be moved through the building at once. At survey in one of these properties, we're checking stair widths and turning space as carefully as we check the room itself, because a narrow period staircase can genuinely limit the size of bath or shower tray that will physically fit through the building — that's something we need to know before a quote is written, not after a bath has arrived and won't go up the stairs. Further out towards the edges of town, the housing is more typically inter-war and post-war family homes, with a scattering of newer residential developments on sites that have been redeveloped over the years. These properties generally give us more straightforward access and more flexibility over where the waste run and supply pipes sit, so the survey here is more focused on the room's own floor and wall build-up than on getting materials through the building. Either way, the survey tells us which situation we're actually dealing with at your address, rather than assuming it from the area.

sections.heading: Booking your survey
sections.body: If you're planning a bathroom installation in Windsor, the survey is the sensible first step whether you already have a design in mind or you're still working out what's possible in the space. We'll come to the property, take the measurements and access checks above, and talk through what you're hoping to achieve — whether that's a full reconfiguration, a wet room conversion, or simply replacing an existing layout with a higher specification. In a Windsor town house close to the centre, that conversation often includes talking through what will and won't fit up the staircase before you commit to a particular bath or shower tray; in a property further out, it's more often about confirming where services can realistically be repositioned. You'll leave the visit with a clear, written scope and a fixed quote for the installation, so you can compare it properly against anything else you're considering, without having to guess at what extra costs might appear later. We fit only — the survey covers what we need to install your bathroom to the specification you've chosen, and we work from your own supplied products or alongside your showroom or designer.

faqs.q: Does the £125 survey fee come off the final price?
faqs.a: Yes. The £125 is a fixed fee for the visit itself, and it's deducted from your total project cost if you go ahead with an installation through us.

faqs.q: Will a narrow Windsor town house staircase limit what bath or shower I can have?
faqs.a: It can. Many of the Georgian and Victorian town houses near the Castle and historic centre have period staircases with limited turning space, which constrains how large an item can be carried up to the bathroom. We check this specifically at survey so it's factored into the quote before anything is ordered, not discovered when a bath won't go up the stairs.

faqs.q: Do I need a design ready before you survey my Windsor property?
faqs.a: No. Some of the Windsor properties we survey already have a finalised showroom or designer plan, and others are still at the idea stage. Either way, we measure the room, check waste and supply, and confirm what's structurally possible before any quote is written.

faqs.q: Does a newer Windsor property survey differently to a period town house?
faqs.a: The things we check are the same — floor and wall build-up, waste position, water pressure and access — but what we find differs. In a newer inter-war, post-war or redeveloped property we're usually confirming service runs with more flexibility over positioning; in an older town house near the centre, access and staircase width tend to be the bigger factor.

faqs.q: What happens if the survey finds a problem with the waste run or access?
faqs.a: We tell you at the survey, not partway through the job. If a waste run needs moving or access is restricted, that's scoped and priced into the written quote you receive, so there are no surprises once fitting starts.

image.heroPrompt: Purpose: hero image for the Windsor bathroom survey page, depicting the pre-installation measuring visit inside a period town house. Subject and action: a spirit level propped against a half-stripped wall beside an open notebook with hand-drawn measurements and a retractable tape measure mid-extension across the floor, the measuring moment itself rather than a finished room. Setting and work-stage: a narrow first-floor bathroom in a Georgian town house near Windsor's historic centre, stripped back to bare plaster with the foot of a period staircase visible through the open doorway, early evening light fading outside a small sash window. Composition: low-angle shot from near the skirting board looking up and across the room toward the doorway, tape measure and notebook filling the foreground, the narrow staircase newel post just visible through the door opening in the background. Light and materials: a single work lamp clipped to a step ladder mixing with the last of the blue evening light through the small window, aged lath-and-plaster wall exposed in patches, worn original floorboards, uneven directional light with hard shadow edges near the lamp and soft fading light near the window. Constraints: no people, no text, no logos, no brand names visible on fixtures, no LED strip lighting anywhere in frame, no catalog-symmetrical staging, no uniform gold colour wash across the whole frame, no plants, florals or candles as styling props, no water shown running, varied and believable surface wear on the stripped plaster and floorboards.
image.heroAlt: A spirit level and tape measure laid out during a bathroom survey in a stripped-back Georgian town house bathroom near Windsor's historic centre, a narrow period staircase visible through the doorway in fading evening light.
